fields.foundation: The Mamluk Sultanate was founded in 1250, when Ayyubid authority in Egypt collapsed. Turanshah, the last Ayyubid sultan of Egypt, was assassinated by the mamluks of his late father, al-Salih Ayyub. These elite slave soldiers, predominantly of Kipchak Turkic origin, had just helped defeat the Seventh Crusade of Louis IX at al-Mansura. Shajar al-Durr, al-Salih's widow, briefly ruled as sultan before opposition from the Abbasid caliph and Syrian Ayyubids led to her marriage to the commander Aybak, who became sultan. The new state was made secure in 1260, when Sultan Qutuz and the Bahri Mamluk commander Baybars defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut. Baybars then seized the throne (r. 1260–1277) and proved the sultanate's military strength by campaigning against both Mongols and Crusader states. Control of Egypt, Syria and the Red Sea gave the sultanate economic and military advantages. What set it apart was that it made a slave-soldier system into a ruling class, renewed by constant new purchases and not by hereditary succession. This allowed power to be consolidated quickly and a durable state to be defended in a volatile region.
fields.socioeconomy: The Mamluk Sultanate's economy joined agriculture, trade and urban administration. Egypt's fertile Nile Valley supported intensive cultivation of cereals, flax and sugar cane, sustained by irrigation works maintained under state supervision. Society was organised as a hierarchy. A ruling class of mamluk emirs held military and political power, while urban merchants, scholars (ulama) and artisans, along with a largely agrarian peasantry, sustained production and exchange. Control of Red Sea ports and the Levant allowed the sultanate to dominate the transit trade in spices, textiles and precious goods between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean. Karimi merchants led this trade, and customs duties yielded substantial revenue. Cities such as Cairo, Alexandria and Damascus became cosmopolitan centres of craftsmanship, scholarship and Islamic law. Land revenue was distributed through the iqta system, which assigned officers the revenues of specific lands in return for military service. By the third reign of al-Nasir Muhammad (r. 1310–1341), Cairo was the largest and wealthiest city of the Islamic world, under a military elite that controlled production, urban life and trade together.
fields.military: The sultanate survived and expanded through its army. The core of the Mamluk forces was a disciplined cavalry of slave soldiers purchased as boys, converted to Islam and trained in barracks schools in horsemanship, lance work and mounted archery, the arts known as furusiyya. Infantry, auxiliary troops and Bedouin contingents supported the cavalry, while fleets operated in the Mediterranean and Red Sea. Mamluk officers also held provincial commands, so that the political and military hierarchies were one, and an extensive network of postal relays and signal beacons allowed rapid communication between Cairo and Syria. Campaigns under Baybars, Qalawun and al-Nasir Muhammad secured Syria and the Hejaz, reduced Makuria in Nubia to vassalage and raided Cilician Armenia, while the victory at Ain Jalut in 1260 and later at Homs and Marj al-Saffar checked Mongol expansion. The army also defeated the Crusader states, ending with al-Ashraf Khalil's capture of Acre in 1291. Soldiers were loyal above all to their master and comrades. Rivalry between the mamluk households of successive sultans therefore bred factionalism, which affected succession and stability throughout the sultanate's history.
fields.governance: In the Mamluk Sultanate an autocratic sultan governed through a developed bureaucracy and the iqta land-grant system. The sultan controlled appointments, military operations and fiscal policy, while provincial governors (na'ibs) and emirs administered Syria and other outlying regions. From 1261 the sultans hosted a line of Abbasid caliphs in Cairo, whose nominal endorsement lent religious legitimacy to rulers of slave origin. The legal system rested on Sunni Islamic law, with chief qadis appointed for each of the four schools, alongside military jurisdiction over mamluk conduct. Civil bureaucracies of scribes and tax officials, often drawn from established civilian and Coptic families, mobilised resources efficiently. Under al-Nasir Muhammad these institutions were at their strongest, with a new cadastral survey (the rawk of 1315), redistribution of iqtas and extensive urban building. After 1382 power passed to the Burji regime of Circassian mamluks under Barquq, but government remained vulnerable to succession crises, factional rivalry and demographic shocks such as the Black Death, which undermined labour and administrative capacity.
fields.impact: The Mamluk Sultanate had a strong influence on the Eastern Mediterranean and the Islamic world. By repelling the Mongols and eliminating the Crusader strongholds, it stabilised the region and became guardian of Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem. Control of Egypt, Syria and the Red Sea routes let it dominate the spice trade between India and Europe until the Portuguese opened the Cape route to India in 1498. Qalawun, al-Nasir Muhammad, Sultan Hasan and later Qaitbay filled Cairo with works of Islamic architecture, while scholars such as Ibn Khaldun, al-Maqrizi and Ibn Hajar made it a centre of learning. Neighbouring Islamic states borrowed from the sultanate's military and administrative model, and its chancery practices set precedents for government in the Eastern Mediterranean. In diplomacy the Mamluk state dealt with the Golden Horde, the Ilkhanate, the Ottomans and European powers such as Venice and Aragon, and it counted for much in regional politics. It lasted long and controlled trade and holy sites, and these affected the economic, military and cultural development of the region.
fields.decline: The decline of the Mamluk Sultanate began in the mid-14th century, under pressure from within and without. Recurrent succession crises after the death of al-Nasir Muhammad in 1341 weakened central authority. The Black Death, which reached Egypt in 1347 and returned repeatedly, caused catastrophic population loss, labour shortages and the decay of irrigation systems, undermining agriculture and state revenue. Timur's sack of Damascus in 1400–1401 devastated Syria. Economic disruption deepened in the early 16th century as the Portuguese contested the Indian Ocean trade, defeating a Mamluk fleet at Diu in 1509 and depriving the sultanate of customs revenue it depended on. Meanwhile, the Ottoman Empire, with its firearms-equipped infantry and artillery, presented a military threat the sultanate could not overcome. Defeat at the Battle of Marj Dabiq in 1516, where Sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri was killed, and at Ridaniya near Cairo in 1517 led to the Ottoman conquest of Egypt under Selim I, ending Mamluk sovereignty. Mamluk households persisted in Egypt under Ottoman rule, but the sultanate ceased to exist as an independent state.
fields.summary: The Mamluk Sultanate turned a slave-soldier corps into a durable ruling state. It halted the Mongols at Ain Jalut, ended the Crusader states, and made Cairo the leading city of the Islamic world until the Ottoman conquest of 1517.
fields.teaser: The Mamluks, former slave soldiers, halted the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut in 1260 and went on to expel the last Crusaders from the Levant. They ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250 until the Ottoman conquest of 1517.
fields.t0: The Mamluk Sultanate was ruled from Cairo by slave soldiers, renewed by fresh purchases rather than hereditary succession.
fields.t1: It halted the Mongols at Ain Jalut, ended the Crusader states and grew rich on the spice trade between India and Europe.
fields.t2: Plague, Portuguese competition at sea and Ottoman guns brought it down, ending with Selim I's conquest of Egypt in 1517.
fields.dyk: Though rulers of slave origin, the Mamluk sultans hosted a line of Abbasid caliphs in Cairo from 1261, whose nominal blessing lent them religious legitimacy.
